title: Brown University President Steps Down After Clashing With Trump Over Federal Funding
excerpt: Christina Paxson, the longest-serving Ivy League president, will leave at the end of the 2026–27 academic year after navigating a $510 million funding freeze and a campus shooting.
body:
• Christina Paxson, Brown University's president since 2012 and the longest-serving Ivy League leader, announced Monday she will step down at the end of the 2026–27 academic year.
  • She extended her planned retirement by a year to navigate a federal funding freeze after the Trump administration threatened to withhold $510 million in research grants over antisemitism allegations.
  • Brown's deal with the White House required the university to invest $50 million in Rhode Island workforce programs and comply with admissions and transgender athlete policies.
  • Paxson rejected a separate Trump "Compact" that would have capped international undergraduate enrollment at 15% — a provision with direct implications for Indian students at elite U.S. universities.

A Presidency Defined by Crisis

Brown University President Christina Paxson announced on Monday that she would step down at the end of the coming academic year, closing a tenure marked by a pandemic, a mass shooting, and an escalating confrontation with the Trump administration over the future of higher education.

Paxson, 66, has led Brown since 2012, making her the longest-serving president in the Ivy League. She had planned to retire a year earlier but extended her stay to steer the university through what she described in an open letter as a "federal funding freeze that imperiled our mission."

"I am proud that we came to an agreement with the federal government that restored our funding while staying true to Brown's values."

— Christina Paxson, President, Brown University

The Funding Battle

Brown was among the first universities targeted during the Trump administration's second-term crackdown on elite institutions. Officials threatened to block $510 million in federal research grants over what the administration called antisemitism tied to pro-Palestinian student protests.

Paxson negotiated a deal in July 2025 that restored the funding. The terms required Brown to commit $50 million over a decade to workforce development in Rhode Island, conduct a third-party evaluation of its campus climate for Jewish students, adopt the administration's definitions of male and female, and comply with policies on transgender athletes. The deal did not restrict curriculum or academic programs.

The agreement drew sharp internal criticism. Students and faculty urged the university to resist federal pressure, and an alumni group gathered over 1,500 petition signatures opposing any concessions. Trump celebrated the deal on Truth Social, writing: "Woke is officially DEAD at Brown."

Rejecting the Compact

Three months later, the Trump administration sent nine elite universities a proposal titled "A Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education." The compact offered preferential federal funding to schools that capped international undergraduate enrollment at 15%, defined gender based on biology, and banned the use of race or sex in admissions and hiring.

Paxson declined. She told Education Secretary Linda McMahon that accepting the compact "would restrict academic freedom and undermine the autonomy of Brown's governance." MIT had rejected the offer a week earlier. None of the nine invitees signed on.

Campus Tragedy

The most devastating event of Paxson's presidency came in December 2025, when a gunman killed two students and injured nine in a lecture-hall attack. The shootings forced a six-day campus lockdown before the suspect was found dead in New Hampshire. The Wall Street Journal reported the incident left an enduring mark on the community and added to the weight of a presidency already tested by the pandemic and political upheaval.

What It Means for Indian Students

Paxson's rejection of the international enrollment cap carried particular weight for Indian students, who represent one of the largest groups of international undergraduates and graduate students at Ivy League universities. Had Brown accepted the 15% threshold, it could have set a precedent for other institutions, potentially narrowing pathways for Indian students seeking admission to top U.S. universities.

The broader question of federal influence over university admissions remains unresolved. Four Ivy League presidents have been pushed out by political pressure since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel — at Penn, Harvard, and twice at Columbia. Paxson's departure, while voluntary, underscores the toll the current environment is exacting on higher education leadership.

Brown's board of trustees will begin a search for her successor. Michael Steinberg, a history professor and president of Brown's chapter of the American Association of University Professors, told the Wall Street Journal that Paxson was "broadly viewed by faculty as an able fundraiser" but that questions remain over the school's ability to navigate the volatile political landscape ahead.
